items.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: my idols were Roy Eldridge and Lester Young... When I heard Bird and Diz I said what is that? Because they played all these technique things... I was trying to learn bebop like Charlie Parker.

ctx.x: She was and old time movie columnist who could make you or break you, you know, in the movie business. She’d be sitting there. It didn’t make any sense that people were coming to see the band. And we were the heroes. We played — $15 a night and our bar tabs were $23. You’ve got to be an idiot to do that. We were having so much fun. We didn’t care about the music. And that went on for about five weeks in a row. It was Mondays, maybe two nights a week. Then the club owner says, “Why don’t we do this five nights a…

tell you what I need now.” I’m the band leader, there was something I wanted to hear. You know, right or wrong, I wanted to hear something that I wanted. It started with, “You hear how the lead trumpet player, how you can hear him so well?” “Yeah.” I said, “Now let me hear the fourth trumpet player. All four trumpets. On the same level.” I wanted to hear the sound of a band, not protruding notes. Now great, now you hear? In the old days, by the way, it was hard to record the bass. All you heard was boom-boom-…

items.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 5, 2021 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: I had a great rapport with Bird... he came and played the next sixteen bars

ctx.x: Okay. Well speaking of ideas, you wrote that when you first tried to play bebop early on that your first note and your last note would be right, and everything in the middle was very questionable.

Well you’ve got to understand, when I first heard Bird and Diz I was home on furlough. And when I heard — I didn’t believe what I was hearing. But I know they were playing double-time, and I was in the Army by the way, I was on furlough. And in the Army I was the drummer with a 38-piece orchestra making all the Army movie pictures. We had a number of drummers in the band so we used to have little jam sessions and I would play vibes, with some of the other drummers playing. And I played straight ahead, you know.…

be George Gershwin. Because everything he played was a song. Everything that came out of that horn, you slow it down and you could write a lyric to it. So my point, getting back to that first note, I heard all those notes so I wanted to play them but I didn’t know what the heck they were doing, so I said the first note I hit was always boom — and I ended up on saying boom. In the middle is [inaudible]. The rhythms were there but not the notes until I came out of the Army and started jamming with players who were…

items.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 5, 2021 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: Teddy Reig was the first guy to ever record Bird and Diz, for Savoy Records... Allen Eager... played with Bird and Diz and Miles and all those people.

ctx.x: Yeah. [inaudible] I think it was my first big record date with Allen Eager. Allen Eager — you know who Teddy “Fats” Reig was? Teddy Reig was the first guy to ever record Bird and Diz, for Savoy Records. He ran that company. And Teddy weighed about 400 pounds. And Allen Eager was the hot white tenor player. He was like the first guy that played like Prez, not that well known. But he had be — he played bebop but like Prez. And he played with Bird and Diz and Miles and all those people. Well Allen loved me and Allen…

Allen said, “You want to play ‘Jordu’?” and I said, “play the melody and I’ll learn” you know. It was really fast. He played it and I played it right after him. And so you know we always played short choruses, maybe 16 bars, because records in those days were three minutes. So but I didn’t know the release chord changes. So I walked over to Duke, who was out in the boonies mentally at the time, he was stoned out, and I said to him, I whispered in his ear, I said, “Duke, what’s the changes in the release?” He…
